_meta.author: Eduventure (original questions)
_meta.note: University batch 1: Programming 10, Computer Science 8, Statistics 10, Calculus 8, Psychology 7, Accounting 7. In review until approved in /admin. Contains answers: never imported by src/.

questions.subject: programming
questions.prompt: In Python 3, what does print(7 // 2) output?
questions.explanation: // is floor division: it divides and rounds down to a whole number. 7 / 2 = 3.5, rounded down to 3.

wrong.c: Floor division rounds down, not to the nearest whole number.

questions.subject: programming
questions.prompt: In Python, what is len([1, [2, 3], 4])?
questions.explanation: The outer list has three elements: 1, the list [2, 3], and 4. len does not count inside the nested list.

mistakes.why: The inner list [2, 3] counts as a single element of the outer list.

questions.subject: programming
questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n items?
questions.explanation: Each step halves the remaining range, so at most about log₂ n steps are needed.

wrong.b: O(n) is linear search, checking items one by one.
wrong.c: O(n log n) is typical of efficient sorting, not searching.
wrong.d: O(1) would mean finding any item in one step regardless of n.

questions.objective: Analyse the complexity of searching algorithms.
questions.alignment: Data structures and algorithms (e.g. first/second-year CS).

questions.subject: programming
questions.prompt: Select all the immutable built-in types in Python.
questions.explanation: Tuples, strings and integers cannot be changed after creation; operations on them create new objects.

wrong.b: Lists are mutable: append, remove and item assignment change them in place.
wrong.d: Dictionaries are mutable: you can add, change and delete keys.

questions.subject: programming
questions.prompt: Put these time complexities in order, from slowest-growing to fastest-growing.
questions.explanation: Constant O(1) does not grow; O(log n) grows very slowly; O(n) grows in step with n; O(n²) grows fastest.
questions.alignment: Data structures and algorithms (e.g. first/second-year CS).

questions.subject: programming
questions.prompt: True or false: in Python, the first element of a list has index 0.
questions.explanation: Python uses zero-based indexing: for x = ['a', 'b'], x[0] is 'a'.

wrong.false: Python, like C and Java, counts from 0. x[1] is the second element.

questions.subject: programming
questions.prompt: After running x = [3, 1, 2] and then x.sort(), what is x[-1]?
questions.explanation: x.sort() sorts in place to [1, 2, 3]. Index −1 is the last element: 3.

mistakes.why: 2 was last before sorting; sort() changes the list in place.
−1 means the last element, not the first.

questions.subject: programming
questions.prompt: What do we call a function that calls itself?
questions.explanation: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem, and needs a base case so that it stops.

questions.subject: programming
questions.prompt: Match each data structure to how it behaves.

right.text: Key–value lookup in average constant time

questions.explanation: A stack is like a pile of plates (LIFO); a queue is like a line at a shop (FIFO); a hash table maps keys to values for fast lookup.
questions.alignment: Data structures and algorithms (e.g. first/second-year CS).

questions.subject: programming
questions.prompt: What does git commit do?

options.text: Records the staged changes as a snapshot in the local repository
Downloads the latest changes from a remote

questions.explanation: A commit saves a snapshot of the staged changes, with a message, in your local history.

wrong.c: Downloading is git fetch or git pull.
wrong.d: Creating a branch is git branch or git switch -c.

questions.alignment: Software development practice (e.g. first-year CS / diploma).

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.prompt: How many different values can be represented with 10 bits?
questions.explanation: Each bit doubles the number of combinations: 2¹⁰ = 1024.

mistakes.why: 20 is 2 × 10; the combinations multiply: 2 × 2 × … (ten times).
1023 is the largest unsigned value; counting 0 as well gives 1024 values.

questions.objective: Relate the number of bits to the number of values.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.prompt: In the TCP/IP model, which layer does HTTP belong to?
questions.explanation: HTTP is an application-layer protocol used by web browsers and servers. It runs on top of TCP (transport) and IP (internet).

wrong.b: The transport layer holds TCP and UDP.
wrong.d: The link layer covers physical networks such as Ethernet and Wi-Fi.

questions.objective: Place protocols in the TCP/IP model.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a valid IPv4 address?
questions.explanation: Each of the four parts of an IPv4 address is one byte, so it must be from 0 to 255. 256 is too big.

wrong.a: 192.168.0.1 is valid (a common private home-network address).
wrong.c: 10.0.0.255 is valid: every part is between 0 and 255.
wrong.d: 8.8.8.8 is valid (a well-known public DNS server).

questions.objective: Recognise the structure of IPv4 addresses.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.prompt: True or false: a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 can be decrypted to recover the original input.
questions.explanation: Hashing is one-way: there is no key and no decryption. That is why systems store password hashes rather than passwords.

wrong.true: Hashing is not encryption. It is designed so that the input cannot be worked out from the hash, other than by guessing.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.prompt: What is the hexadecimal number FF in decimal?
questions.explanation: F = 15. FF = 15 × 16 + 15 = 240 + 15 = 255, the largest value of one byte.

mistakes.why: 30 adds the digits; the left F is worth 15 × 16.
256 is 16²; FF is one less.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.prompt: Select all the logic gates that output 1 when both inputs are 1.
questions.explanation: AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1. OR gives 1 when at least one is 1.

wrong.c: NAND is NOT-AND: with both inputs 1 it outputs 0.
wrong.d: XOR outputs 1 only when the inputs differ.
wrong.e: NOR outputs 1 only when both inputs are 0.

questions.alignment: Digital logic and computer organisation (e.g. first-year CS).

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.prompt: Put these types of storage in order from fastest to slowest access.
questions.explanation: Registers sit inside the CPU core, cache is on the chip, RAM is on the motherboard and an SSD is external storage. Faster memory is smaller and more expensive.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.prompt: How many bits are there in one byte?
questions.explanation: A byte is 8 bits, enough for 256 different values (0–255).

mistakes.why: 4 bits is a nibble, half a byte.

questions.subject: statistics
questions.prompt: A and B are mutually exclusive, with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A or B)?
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.7.

mistakes.why: 0.12 is P(A) × P(B), which would be P(A and B) for independent events, not P(A or B).
There is no overlap to subtract: P(A and B) = 0 for mutually exclusive events.

questions.objective: Apply the addition rule for mutually exclusive events.

questions.subject: statistics
questions.prompt: What is the expected value of the score when a fair six-sided die is rolled?
questions.explanation: E[X] = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) ÷ 6 = 21 ÷ 6 = 3.5. It need not be a possible outcome.

mistakes.why: The expected value is the mean, 3.5; it does not have to be a whole number.

questions.objective: Calculate the expected value of a discrete random variable.

questions.subject: statistics
questions.prompt: For a normal distribution, about what percentage of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explanation: The empirical (68–95–99.7) rule: about 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD and 99.7% within 3 SD.

wrong.d: 50% of values lie on each side of the mean, not within one SD.

questions.subject: statistics
questions.prompt: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads? (Give a decimal.)
questions.explanation: There are 8 equally likely outcomes, and 3 have exactly two heads (HHT, HTH, THH). 3/8 = 0.375.

mistakes.why: 0.25 is (1/2)², ignoring the third toss and the 3 orders.
1/8 is one particular order; there are 3 orders with two heads.

questions.subject: statistics
questions.prompt: True or false: if two variables are strongly correlated, one must cause the other.
questions.explanation: Correlation shows variables move together, not why. A third factor may drive both (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in hot weather), or it may be chance.

wrong.true: Correlation alone cannot establish causation; that needs controlled experiments or careful causal reasoning.

questions.subject: statistics
questions.prompt: A test gives p = 0.03 at the 5% significance level. What is the correct conclusion?

options.text: The null hypothesis has a 3% chance of being true

questions.explanation: Since p < 0.05, results this extreme would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true, so we reject it at the 5% level.

wrong.b: A p-value is the probability of the data (or more extreme) given the null, not the probability that the null is true.
wrong.c: p-values do not give the probability that a hypothesis is true.
wrong.d: Significance is not size: a tiny effect can be significant with a large sample.

questions.subject: statistics
questions.prompt: Var(X) = 3. What is Var(2X)?
questions.explanation: Var(aX) = a² Var(X) = 4 × 3 = 12.

mistakes.why: Variance scales by the square of the constant: 2² = 4, not 2.

questions.subject: statistics
questions.prompt: Select all the measures of spread.
questions.explanation: Range, standard deviation and interquartile range describe how spread out data are.

wrong.b: The mean is a measure of centre.
wrong.e: The mode is a measure of centre (the most common value).

questions.objective: Distinguish measures of centre and spread.

questions.subject: statistics
questions.prompt: Match each variable to its type of data.
questions.explanation: Eye colour has categories with no order (nominal). Sizes have a natural order (ordinal). Height can take any value in a range (continuous).
questions.objective: Classify variables by level of measurement.

questions.subject: statistics
questions.prompt: Find the median of 3, 9, 1, 7, 5, 11.
questions.explanation: Sort the data: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. With an even count, the median is the mean of the middle two: (5 + 7) ÷ 2 = 6.

mistakes.why: Sort the data before finding the middle.
With six values, average the two middle ones (5 and 7).

questions.objective: Find the median of a data set.

questions.subject: calculus
questions.prompt: If f(x) = x³ − 2x, what is f′(1)?

mistakes.why: −1 is f(1) = 1 − 2; differentiate first, then substitute.

questions.subject: calculus
questions.prompt: What is the derivative of ln x (for x > 0)?
questions.explanation: d/dx (ln x) = 1/x.

wrong.b: Only eˣ is its own derivative, not ln x.
wrong.c: eˣ is the derivative of eˣ, the inverse function of ln x.
wrong.d: x ln x − x is the integral of ln x.

questions.subject: calculus
questions.prompt: Evaluate the integral of sin x from x = 0 to x = π.
questions.explanation: ∫ sin x dx = −cos x. From 0 to π: (−cos π) − (−cos 0) = 1 + 1 = 2.

mistakes.why: 0 is the integral from 0 to 2π, where positive and negative areas cancel.

questions.objective: Evaluate definite integrals of trigonometric functions.

questions.subject: calculus
questions.prompt: Differentiate x·eˣ.
questions.explanation: Product rule: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′ = 1·eˣ + x·eˣ = eˣ(x + 1).

wrong.b: That multiplies the derivatives (1 × eˣ); the product rule adds two terms.
wrong.d: The second term should be x·eˣ, not x.

questions.subject: calculus
questions.prompt: What is the limit of (sin x)/x as x approaches 0 (x in radians)?
questions.explanation: For small x (in radians), sin x ≈ x, so (sin x)/x → 1. It can be shown with the squeeze theorem.

mistakes.why: Both top and bottom go to 0, but their ratio approaches 1.

questions.subject: calculus
questions.prompt: True or false: if f′(a) = 0, then f must have a maximum or a minimum at x = a.
questions.explanation: f(x) = x³ has f′(0) = 0, but x = 0 is a point of inflection, not a maximum or minimum.

wrong.true: A zero derivative only means a stationary point. Check the sign change of f′ (or f″) to classify it: x³ at 0 is a counter-example.

questions.subject: calculus
questions.prompt: At what x-value does y = x² − 6x + 5 have its stationary point?
questions.explanation: dy/dx = 2x − 6 = 0 gives x = 3 (a minimum, since the x² coefficient is positive).

mistakes.why: Solve 2x − 6 = 0: x = 3, not 6.
−4 is the y-value at the stationary point; the question asks for x.

questions.subject: calculus
questions.prompt: What is the indefinite integral of 1/x?
questions.explanation: d/dx ln|x| = 1/x, so ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c. The power rule cannot be used here because n = −1.

wrong.b: The power rule fails for n = −1: it would divide by zero.
wrong.c: −1/x² is the derivative of 1/x, not its integral.

questions.subject: psychology
questions.prompt: In Pavlov's experiments, after conditioning, what is the bell?
questions.explanation: The bell was neutral at first. After being paired with food, it triggers salivation by itself, making it a conditioned (learned) stimulus.

wrong.b: The food is the unconditioned stimulus: it causes salivation without learning.
wrong.c: Salivating to food is the unconditioned response.
wrong.d: Salivating to the bell is the conditioned response; the bell itself is a stimulus.

questions.objective: Apply the terms of classical conditioning.

questions.subject: psychology
questions.prompt: Put the levels of Maslow's hierarchy of needs in order, from the base of the pyramid to the top.
questions.explanation: Physiological (food, sleep) → safety → love and belonging → esteem → self-actualisation.

questions.subject: psychology
questions.prompt: In Piaget's theory, in which stage do people first become able to reason abstractly and hypothetically?
questions.explanation: The formal operational stage (from about age 11–12) brings abstract and hypothetical thinking.

wrong.b: In the concrete operational stage, logic works on concrete, real objects.
wrong.c: The preoperational stage features symbolic play and egocentrism.
wrong.d: The sensorimotor stage (birth to about 2) is about learning through senses and movement.

questions.objective: Describe Piaget's stages of cognitive development.

questions.subject: psychology
questions.prompt: True or false: short-term memory can hold an unlimited amount of information.
questions.explanation: Short-term memory has a small capacity: classic estimates are about 7 ± 2 items (newer research suggests nearer 4 chunks), held for under a minute without rehearsal.

wrong.true: Long-term memory has a very large capacity, but short-term memory is strictly limited.

questions.objective: Describe the capacity of short-term memory.

questions.subject: psychology
questions.prompt: Match each research method to its description.

right.text: Questionnaires or interviews given to many people
Changes one variable to measure its effect on another
An in-depth study of one person or group

questions.explanation: Experiments manipulate an independent variable; case studies go deep on one case; surveys collect self-reports from many people.
questions.alignment: Introductory psychology: research methods (e.g. first-year university).

questions.subject: psychology
questions.prompt: Select all the traits that are part of the Big Five model of personality.
questions.explanation: The Big Five are openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism (OCEAN).

wrong.c: Intelligence is a cognitive ability, measured separately from the Big Five.
wrong.e: Happiness is a mood or well-being measure, not one of the five traits.

questions.objective: Identify the Big Five personality traits.

questions.subject: psychology
questions.prompt: What is the name of the tendency to look for and favour information that supports what we already believe?
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias leads people to notice, seek and remember evidence that fits their existing beliefs, and to discount evidence against them.

questions.subject: accounting
questions.prompt: Which is the accounting equation?
questions.explanation: Everything a business owns (assets) is financed either by what it owes (liabilities) or by the owners (equity).

wrong.b: Equity is added, not subtracted: both liabilities and equity finance the assets.
wrong.c: Revenue and expenses belong in the income statement, not this equation.

questions.alignment: Introductory financial accounting (e.g. first-year university / diploma).

questions.subject: accounting
questions.prompt: A business has assets of RM50,000 and liabilities of RM20,000. What is its equity, in ringgit?
questions.explanation: Equity = Assets − Liabilities = 50,000 − 20,000 = RM30,000.

mistakes.why: Equity is what is left after liabilities: subtract, do not add.

questions.alignment: Introductory financial accounting (e.g. first-year university / diploma).

questions.subject: accounting
questions.prompt: A bank loan repayable in 5 years is classified as a…
questions.explanation: It is money owed (a liability) and is due after more than 12 months, so it is non-current.

wrong.b: The loan is owed by the business, so it is a liability, not an asset.
wrong.c: Equity is the owners' stake; a loan is owed to an outside lender.
wrong.d: Only the interest on the loan is an expense; the loan itself is a liability.

questions.objective: Classify items in the statement of financial position.
questions.alignment: Introductory financial accounting (e.g. first-year university / diploma).

questions.subject: accounting
questions.prompt: True or false: in double-entry bookkeeping, every transaction is recorded as a debit in one account and a matching credit in another.
questions.explanation: Each transaction affects at least two accounts with equal debits and credits, which keeps the accounting equation in balance.

wrong.false: That is the core rule of double entry: total debits always equal total credits.

questions.alignment: Introductory financial accounting (e.g. first-year university / diploma).

questions.subject: accounting
questions.prompt: A machine costs RM10,000, has a residual value of RM2,000 and a useful life of 4 years. What is the annual straight-line depreciation, in ringgit?
questions.explanation: Depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life = (10,000 − 2,000) ÷ 4 = RM2,000 per year.

mistakes.why: Subtract the residual value first: (10,000 − 2,000) ÷ 4.

questions.alignment: Introductory financial accounting (e.g. first-year university / diploma).

questions.subject: accounting
questions.prompt: Select all the current assets.
questions.explanation: Current assets are expected to be turned into cash or used within 12 months: inventory, receivables and cash.

wrong.c: Machinery is used for many years: a non-current asset.
wrong.e: Buildings are long-term: a non-current asset.

questions.alignment: Introductory financial accounting (e.g. first-year university / diploma).

questions.subject: accounting
questions.prompt: Sales are RM80,000 and the cost of sales is RM50,000. What is the gross profit, in ringgit?
questions.explanation: Gross profit = sales − cost of sales = 80,000 − 50,000 = RM30,000.

mistakes.why: Gross profit subtracts the cost of sales from sales.

questions.alignment: Introductory financial accounting (e.g. first-year university / diploma).
